transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-22
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~78 minutes
Platform: Zoom (recording + local notes)
Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Iris (Redwood Solutions Eng), Jordan (Redwood Product), Carlos (SDA Eng Mgr), Leila (ML Infra), Tom (Senior ML Eng), Priya (Sec Arch)

Summary:
- Deep dive on how to run apples-to-apples runtime benchmarks for SDA Telecom pilot: prompt sets, load-generation fidelity, warmup, KV cache hit-rate, batching profiles, and quantization variants.
- Agreed to exchange artifacts: load generator, canonical prompts, current prod traces.
- Next steps include shared benchmark run and a follow-up to compare p95/p99 and throughput across hosted vs dedicated vs on-prem configs.

Topics:
- Benchmark design (prompt stratification, latency metrics, p50/p95/p99, tail)
- Load generation (rps vs open-loop, concurrency, think time, client bottlenecks)
- Runtime knobs (batching windows, continuous batching, max batch size, prefetech)
- KV cache behavior (prefix cache vs KV cache, eviction, cache priming)
- Quantization & perf (fp16 vs int8 vs int4 tradeoffs, quality checks)
- Network topology (VPC peering, NAT, egress bandwidth impact on latency)
- On-prem differences (kernel versions, MIG/partitioning, power gov, device driver variants)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Sofia (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We'll run through a lab-style bench approach — try to get apples-to-apples comparisons across your current infra and our Dedicated / Private options.
[00:28] Carlos (SDA): Cool, yeah we've been trying to figure out why the tail latency spikes when we push more than, like, 350 concurrent sessions.
[00:45] Marcus (SE): Right, and quick note, when we say "tail" we'll focus on p95/p99 plus the token-level tail — sometimes per-token latency tells a different story than request-level.
[01:12] Leila (ML Infra): Can you define token-level tail? I mean, we usually just look at request latency.
[01:22] Marcus (SE): Sure — token-level is how long it takes to produce individual tokens once the request hits the model. If KV cache hit-rate drops, later tokens can take longer, so request p95/p99 increases even if initial tokens look ok.
[01:45] Tom (Customer): We use a small prefix cache in prod, we call it "K-V cash" in some notes, ha — so priming is inconsistent.
[01:55] Iris (Redwood): (laughs) K-V cash, I like that. But yeah, consistent priming during the benchmark is key — we usually recommend an explicit cache warmup phase with representative prompts.
[02:20] Jordan (Product): Also want to capture batching behavior. If your client sends many short prompts simultaneously, continuous batching in the runtime may kick in differently than in your current infra. So the load generator needs to mimic real-world concurrency and jitter.
[02:50] Priya (Sec): From security side, we need to know what network hops are in scope — VPC peering or a private link? That affects latency and TLS termination, and the benchmark needs to reflect the chosen topology.
[03:15] Marcus (SE): Good point — for apples-to-apples, we recommend running the same job under three topologies: 1) Hosted (internet path), 2) Dedicated (VPC peering), 3) Private/on-prem (local network), because network egress and NAT can add 10-40ms depending on route.
[03:45] Carlos: Ok. For prompt sets, we have three classes: short status queries (~20 tokens), config patches (~150 tokens), and conversational sessions (~700 tokens). We'll share examples.
[04:05] Marcus: Perfect. We'll also stratify by token length to observe kernel selection and memory pressure effects — sequence length has big impact on kernel choice and batch effectiveness.
[04:30] Tom: For load generation — are we doing closed-loop or open-loop? We currently use an open-loop stress test on our side.
[04:44] Iris: Open-loop is fine to push high RPS, but closed-loop (where you wait for responses before sending next) better reflects user-perceived latency. We recommend running both: closed-loop for SLA checks and open-loop for throughput saturation.
[05:10] Leila: How do you handle batching windows? If we set batch window to 10ms vs 50ms we saw big differences in p50 but tradeoffs in p99.
[05:28] Marcus: Exactly — batch window and max batch size are tuning knobs. We'll instrument per-batch size distribution and latency per batch. Redwood runtime supports adaptive batching: it favors low latency but will grow batch size under load. We'll capture that distribution in the benchmark output.
[05:55] Priya: For the quantization tests — we need an apples-to-apples model. Do you run the same model weights across int8/int4?
[06:05] Marcus: We use the same base FP16 weights then apply quantization pipelines. For int8 vs int4 you can see 1.8x-3x perf improvement in tokens/sec but quality delta can vary; we'll include quality checks (BLEU/style metrics, instruction-following tests) on the canonical prompt sets.
[06:40] Tom: Any tips for the eval harness? We have an eval suite that runs 500 prompts and scores semantics, but it sometimes flattens small degradations.
[06:55] Iris: Add 'sensitive' prompts — prompts that historically showed regressions with aggressive quantization. Also track log-prob deltas, and on a few prompts capture full token-by-token generation to compare.
[07:15] Carlos: Regarding KV cache — what do you recommend for eviction sim? Our cache size is limited and eviction happens during long sessions.
[07:28] Marcus: Two things: 1) Include long-session scenarios in your prompt set to stress eviction and 2) report cache hit ratio per time bucket. We'll simulate eviction by running long multi-turn sessions and measuring per-token latency as conversation length increases.
[07:50] Jordan: Note — in Dedicated we expose cache config options so you can pin prefix caching or extend cache memory depending on GPU footprint.
[08:05] Leila: We'll want to measure warm vs cold start. Cold starts are painful when autoscaling; what does Redwood define as cold?
[08:18] Marcus: Cold usually means no warm-up of model weights or empty caches and no pre-initialized JIT kernels; for hosted infra warm start is typically < 1s but on-prem cold could be tens of seconds depending on container startup. For benchmark, we'll do explicit cold start runs (fresh container) and warm runs (after a sustained warmup period).
[08:42] Tom: Any particular metrics we should collect inside the runtime? We currently just pull request latency and GPU utilization.
[08:52] Iris: Capture per-step kernel times, batch size distribution, KV cache hit rates, GPU memory free, and per-GPU SM occupancy if possible. We'll provide a Grafana dashboard template.
[09:18] Carlos: What about load gen tooling? We have some JMeter scripts but they don't support token-streaming well.
[09:28] Marcus: We can share a Node-based load-generator that supports streaming responses (SSE/WebSocket) and token-level timing. That'll be important to measure tail latency for streamed chat use-cases.
[09:50] Sofia: Quick interruption — for the pilot SOW we usually include a sample bench run: two-week benchmark window, three topologies, three model configs (FP16 baseline, int8 quant, int4 quant), and quality gates. Are you ok with that scope, Carlos?
[10:10] Carlos: Sounds reasonable. We'll need to budget cycles to prepare the prompts and provide a staging VPC.
[10:20] Priya: On the compliance side, we'll need audit logs and KMS integration for any sample data; can you produce redacted logs?
[10:32] Jordan: Yes — we can produce audit logs with PII redaction; for Private/on-prem we'll hand off a module that writes logs to customer-managed S3 with KMS. We'll include that in the doc pack.
[10:55] Tom: When you say "apples-to-apples" what are the big gotchas we should be aware of?
[11:05] Marcus: Common gotchas: mismatched prompt tokenization (different tokenizers yield different token counts), network topology differences, different model configs (hidden dims or layer fusion), and inconsistent warmup or cache priming. Also watch out for client-side limits — some client gateways serialize requests unintentionally.
[11:40] Leila: Tokenization hits me — our current tokenization pipeline applies a pre-processing step that strips stopwords. We should standardize tokenization for the bench.
[11:55] Iris: We'll provide tokenizer scripts and a token-counting spec so both sides measure tokens the same way.
[12:10] Marcus: Good. Also we'll produce a 'manifest' JSON for each prompt set describing expected tokens, LF counts, and a category label so we can stratify results.
[12:30] Carlos: Will you also test per-instance locality? We have NUMA concerns when multiple model instances run on the same host.
[12:42] Marcus: Yes — in on-prem config we'll run with different placement strategies (one instance per GPU vs multi-instance) and capture NUMA-bound artifacts. We'll include a small script to pin CPU/GPU affinities.
[13:05] Tom: How long should the warmup be? If we do 5 minutes warmup is that enough?
[13:16] Iris: Depends on workload — for large models with lazy kernel JIT you might want 10-15 minutes to get stable steady-state. We'll recommend monitoring rolling p95 to determine stabilization.
[13:40] Priya: Anything we need to change for our restricted environment? We run hardened kernels and FIPS mode.
[13:50] Marcus: We'll document driver/kernel compatibility matrix. FIPS and certain cipher suites can add TLS overhead; we'll recommend running the benchmark both with your hardened stack and a 'reference' stack so delta is visible.
[14:08] Carlos: I want to capture cost signals too — tokens/sec per USD and p95 dollars per successful response. Can Redwood expose cost estimates?
[14:20] Jordan: Yes, Redwood Optimize can provide per-token cost breakdowns given model/quantization config and observed throughput. For Dedicated pilot we'll produce a cost model based on your projected 24/7 load.
[14:40] Tom: For the quantization quality baseline, do you keep a golden FP16 run and diff outputs?
[14:50] Marcus: Exactly — golden FP16 run with deterministic seeds when possible, then compute token-level diffs, semantic metrics, and a human evaluation sample for instruction following.
[15:12] Leila: We'll need to validate reproducibility — how deterministic are runs in your runtime?
[15:22] Marcus: We can enable deterministic sampling for bench (fixed RNG seeds); but note some kernel fusions and non-deterministic gather ops can introduce small diffs; we log seed + env to help trace.
[15:42] Sofia: Let's capture the exact artifacts we will exchange after this call. Marcus?
[15:50] Marcus: I'll share: 1) load-generator repo (Node + JMeter wrappers), 2) benchmark dashboard and templates, 3) tokenizer scripts and prompt manifest, 4) sample SOW. I'll upload to the shared drive and post the link.
[16:10] Tom: We'll share: 1) three prompt sets, 2) current p95/p99 traces, 3) VPC peering details and test CIDRs.
[16:28] Priya: I'll send a redacted compliance checklist and KMS requirements.
[16:40] Sofia: Great. Any final questions?
[16:45] Carlos: One last thing — how do you account for bursty traffic and cold-snap autoscaling? We occasionally get sudden spikes.
[16:55] Iris: We'll run synthetic bursts in open-loop and measure cold start tail. Also will test warm-pool sizing for Dedicated to see tradeoffs between cost and instantaneous capacity.
[17:10] Leila: Can you simulate multi-tenant noise? We sometimes have other workloads on the same host.
[17:20] Marcus: For Dedicated we can simulate co-located CPU/GPU noise by running background stressors during some runs, but for true isolation we compare against private on-prem where tenant noise is controlled by you.
[17:45] Carlos: Ok that helps, thanks.

[18:00] Recap (Sofia): Action list: Marcus shares artifacts; customer shares prompts and traces; schedule follow-up bench kickoff week of 2025-04-28. We'll aim to have a baseline report within two weeks of bench completion.
[18:30] End of call.
